summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

primary_citations.citation_text: Michigan - Michigan Compiled Laws § 722.621 et seq. (Child Protection Law – mandatory reporting)
Michigan - Michigan Court Rules, Subchapter 3.900 (Proceedings Involving Juveniles – child protective proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court conditionally reversed for ICWA-notice violations, holding that almost any indicium of tribal membership triggers 25 USC 1912(a) notice, that a parent cannot waive the tribe's independent rights, and that the trial court must maintain a documentary record of notice and proof of service.
key_cases.relevance: Morris sets Michigan's very low threshold for ICWA notice and makes the trial court responsible for documenting that notice was actually served.
key_cases.quote: we hold that virtually any criteria on which tribal membership might be based suffices to trigger the 25 USC 1912(a) notice requirement

key_cases.holding: The Court held that a parent of an Indian child who executes a consent under MCL 712B.13 of MIFPA may withdraw it any time before a final adoption order, even in a child protective proceeding, although the department may then refile under MCL 712B.15.
key_cases.relevance: MIFPA and ICWA apply together in Michigan, and a parent of an Indian child keeps MIFPA's withdrawal right even inside a child protective case.
key_cases.quote: He was therefore entitled to withdraw his consent at any time before entry of a final order of adoption.

key_cases.holding: The Court held MIFPA's special protections applied to the child taken from the mother's care even though she was placed with a relative, and vacated for non-compliance, but held they did not apply to the sibling the mother voluntarily placed with his non-respondent father.
key_cases.relevance: Detmer defines what counts as a 'removal' that triggers MIFPA in Michigan, including a removal into relative care.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the special protections set forth in the Michigan Indian Family Preservation Act do apply to AB's removal

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of parental rights to two Indian children because the trial court's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt finding of likely serious harm was not supported by the qualified-expert-witness testimony ICWA and MIFPA require.
key_cases.relevance: The qualified expert witness is a mandatory component of the evidentiary finding in every Michigan ICWA/MIFPA termination.
key_cases.quote: in order to terminate parental rights to an Indian child, a trial court's "beyond a reasonable doubt" finding must "contain" or "encompass" testimony of a qualified expert witness

search_keywords: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

state_agency.name: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, dentists, physician's assistants, registered dental hygienists, medical examiners, nurses, and persons licensed to provide emergency medical care — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(a)
Audiologists, psychologists, physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and athletic trainers

Marriage and family therapists, licensed professional counselors, social workers, licensed master's social workers, licensed bachelor's social workers, registered social service technicians, and social service technicians
Persons employed in a professional capacity in any office of the friend of the court
School administrators, school counselors, and teachers

MDHHS eligibility specialists, family independence managers, family independence specialists, social services specialists, social work specialists, social work specialist managers, and welfare services specialists — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(b)
Employees of an organization that federal funding statutes, regulations, or contracts would otherwise bar from reporting absent a state mandate — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(c)
Not universal: any other person, including a child, MAY report but is not required to — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624
reporting_details: Michigan is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals and MDHHS employees listed in Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1) must report, and they must report immediately to MDHHS centralized intake by telephone or through the Michigan Online Reporting System. A telephone report must be followed within 72 hours by a written report on form DHS-3200, faxed or emailed to Centralized Intake; a report filed through the online reporting system that contains the information required by Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(2) counts as the written report, and MDHHS states that reporting online eliminates the requirement to fill out a DHS-3200 form. Any other person may report voluntarily under Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: MDHHS centralized intake receives the report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.628(1) requires the department, within 24 hours of receiving a report, to refer it to the prosecuting attorney and local law enforcement or to commence an investigation.
Not specified; MDHHS states CPS has 30 days to complete an investigation unless extenuating circumstances require an extension.
